results.title: Sage Research Methods - Encyclopedia of Survey Research Methods - Intercoder Reliability
results.content: Intercoder reliability refers to the extent to which two or more independent coders agree on the coding of the content of interest with an application of the same coding scheme. Intercoder reliability is a critical component in the content analysis of open-ended survey responses, without which the interpretation of the content cannot be considered objective and valid, although high intercoder reliability is not the only criteria necessary to argue that coding is valid. Intercoder reliability is a standard measure of research quality, and a low level of intercoder reliability may suggest weakness in coding methods, including poor operational definitions with unclear coding categories and poor coder training. Although there are more than 30 different statistical measures or indices of intercoder reliability, only a handful of measures are widely used and there is no consensus on the single best measure. Percent agreement is also limited to nominal coding with only two coders with the same number of coded units.

results.title: Intercoder Reliability in Qualitative Research — Delve
results.content: # Intercoder Reliability in Qualitative Research. **This is part of our** **Guide to Collaborative Qualitative Analysis** **|** **Start a Free Trial of Delve** **|** **Take Our Free Online Qualitative Data Analysis Course**. ### Intercoder reliability is like a master recipe for team-based qualitative research. Intercoder reliability is core to a consistent and dependable team effort. This article introduces intercoder reliability for consistent coding – why you need it, which type to choose, and how to do it. The first step before measuring intercoder reliability is collecting and coding your interviews or other qualitative data: identifying and labeling meaningful patterns in your research documents. Whether you’re doing solo research or collaborative qualitative analysis, coding is a core part of the understanding process. Richards (2009) explains that intercoder agreement shows that you (yourself) are “reliably interpreting a code in the same way across time, or that you can rely on your colleagues to use it in the same way.” Testing and tracking how consistently you code is a trust-building activity.
